lesson.title: Counting Energy Storage Elements: Why First-Order Matters
lesson.summary: A first-order circuit is any circuit whose behavior reduces to a single differential equation with one time constant, which happens whenever the circuit contains, after simplification, exactly one independent energy storage element.
lesson.body:
Every circuit studied in this chapter so far, RC charging, RC discharging, RL energizing, RL de-energizing, all share a hidden feature: each one is governed by a differential equation with exactly one derivative in it, and exactly one time constant shows up in the solution. Circuits with this property are called first-order circuits, and the name comes directly from the order of the differential equation that describes them, which in turn is set by how many independent places the circuit has to store energy.

The key word is independent. If a circuit has two capacitors, but they are connected purely in series or purely in parallel with nothing else tapping into the node between them, they can always be combined into a single equivalent capacitance, Ceq, using the same series and parallel rules from ordinary capacitance analysis. Once combined, the circuit is back down to one energy storage element, so it is still first order even though it started out looking like it had two capacitors. The same logic applies to multiple inductors that combine into a single Leq. A circuit only becomes second order, the subject of the next section on damping ratio, when it has two energy storage elements that genuinely cannot be merged into one, most commonly a capacitor and an inductor together in the same loop.

This classification is not just bookkeeping, it tells you in advance exactly what kind of answer to expect. A first-order circuit's natural response is always a single decaying exponential, x_n(t) = x_n(0)*e^(-t/tau), and it can never oscillate or overshoot, because there is only one energy storage mode for the circuit's state to move through on its way to the final value. Every RC and RL example already worked through in this chapter obeys this rule: the response climbs or decays smoothly and monotonically, never ringing past its target the way a second-order RLC circuit can.

As a concrete check, consider two capacitors in series, C1 = 2 microfarads and C2 = 3 microfarads, both fed through a single resistor R = 10 k ohms. Even though there are two physical capacitors, they share only the two nodes of the series connection and nothing else taps between them, so they combine into one equivalent capacitance: Ceq = (C1*C2)/(C1+C2) = (2*3)/(2+3) = 6/5 = 1.2 microfarads. The circuit is still first order, with a single time constant tau = R*Ceq = 10,000 ohms*1.2e-6 F = 0.012 seconds, or 12 milliseconds, computed exactly the same way as for a single capacitor.

Underneath all of this is one governing differential equation shape, dx/dt + x/tau = f(t)/tau, where x is whatever voltage or current the circuit is tracking and f(t) represents the source driving it. Every RC and RL circuit in this chapter, no matter how the resistors and reactive elements were arranged, reduces to this same equation once the time constant is identified, which is exactly why the general exponential response formula from before was able to solve all of them with the same three ingredients: an initial value, a final value, and tau.
